title: Agriculture in the Economy of the Philippines: Jobs, Crops and Challenges
metaTitle: Agriculture in the Economy: Philippine Farm Facts for 2026
metaDescription: Agriculture in the economy of the Philippines: its share of GDP and jobs from the latest PSA data, the main crops, the challenges and what crop yields mean.
excerpt: Agriculture in the economy of the Philippines is small in pesos but huge in people. It makes less than a tenth of the country's output, yet it employs about one in five working Filipinos. Here are the latest PSA numbers, the crops that carry the sector, the problems that hold farms back, and what a farmer can control on the ground.

heroImage.alt: Aerial view of farm fields laid out in patches of green and brown

blocks.text: How big is agriculture in the economy?

The PSA counts farming, forestry and fishing together as one industry, AFF for short. In 2025, AFF produced about PHP 2.41 trillion out of a PHP 28.01 trillion economy at current prices. By our own sum of PSA's four quarterly figures, that is about 8.6 percent of GDP, down from about 9.1 percent in 2024.

The share keeps sliding partly because the rest of the economy grows faster, not because farms produce less. At constant 2018 prices, farm output grew about 3.1 percent in 2025, while the whole economy grew about 4.4 percent. In the second quarter of 2026, for example, AFF still grew 2.7 percent year on year. Even so, at constant 2018 prices it made up only 7.5 percent of GDP in that quarter, the smallest of the three major industries. That figure uses constant prices, so do not set it beside the 8.6 percent at current prices.

Jobs tell a different story. In the July 2026 Labor Force Survey, agriculture employed 19.7 percent of the 49.21 million working Filipinos, or roughly 9.7 million people.

So about a fifth of workers produce less than a tenth of the output. That means output per farm worker sits well below the national average. It also means that every peso of extra yield or saved cost on a farm reaches a large share of Filipino households.

blocks.text: The crops and products that carry the sector

Crops make up the biggest part of farm output. In the second quarter of 2026, crops accounted for 55.0 percent of the value of production in agriculture and fisheries. Poultry followed with 17.7 percent, then livestock with 13.7 percent and fisheries with 13.6 percent.

Palay leads the crops. It was the top contributor to AFF growth in that quarter, with a 5.7 percent rise, while corn grew 0.8 percent. After rice and corn come coconut, banana, sugarcane, mango, pineapple, cassava, coffee, cacao and abaca. For the two staples, see our guides to [palay](/crops/palay) and [pagtatanim ng mais](/crops/pagtatanim-ng-mais). Export crops have their own pages too, such as [banana farming](/crops/banana-farming-philippines).

Weather comes first. Typhoons, floods and dry spells hit the same months that farmers plant and harvest, and a single storm can flatten a field a week before harvest. Some crops also slipped in 2026. In the second quarter, sugarcane fell 22.5 percent, rubber 16.4 percent and banana 4.0 percent from a year earlier.

Next come costs. Fertilizer, fuel, seed and hired labor are all paid in cash, often on credit, long before the harvest comes in. Then the farmer sells at the farmgate price, which swings from season to season and is usually far below the retail price of rice. Our page on [palay prices in the Philippines](/blog/palay-price-philippines) tracks those swings.

Finally, timing matters. PSA projects that palay output for July to September 2026 may drop 15.0 percent from a year earlier, mostly because the harvested area may shrink by 15.8 percent. Yield per hectare, on the other hand, may rise slightly. In other words, fewer hectares, not weaker plants, drive most of that dip.
Fertilizer in agriculture: the biggest input you control

Fertilizer in agriculture does one job: it puts back the nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium that each harvest takes away. Without enough of it, yields usually fall. But too much is money thrown into the mud, because the crop cannot use more than it needs and the rest washes away.

So the best savings come from the right rate at the right stage. First, test your soil or use the recommendation for your area. Next, split nitrogen into two or three doses timed to the crop's growth. Then record what you actually applied, lot by lot. Our guides to [fertilizer for rice](/blog/fertilizer-for-rice), [urea fertilizer](/blog/urea-fertilizer) and [fertilizer calculation](/blog/fertilizer-calculation) walk through each step.
Agricultural engineer hiring and farm jobs

The sector needs more than hands in the field. Irrigation, farm machines, dryers, mills and cold storage all need engineers. Republic Act 10915, the Philippine Agricultural and Biosystems Engineering Act of 2016, requires government agencies, local governments, irrigation systems, rice mills, feed mills and machinery firms to employ licensed agricultural and biosystems engineers.

That law is a steady driver of agricultural engineer hiring in the Philippines, from the Department of Agriculture down to the town hall. If you are weighing the course, read our guide to the [agricultural engineer career](/blog/agricultural-engineer-career), with the board exam, the jobs and the pay.
Ani and crop yields: what the numbers mean

Ani is the Tagalog word for harvest, and it also means the yield itself. Crop yield is the harvest per hectare, usually in metric tons. For July to September 2025, PSA recorded an average palay yield of 4.09 metric tons per hectare. That is about 82 bags of 50 kilograms each. Corn in the same period averaged 3.07 metric tons per hectare.

Those are national averages, so many farms do better and many do worse. The gap between them comes from variety, water, fertilizer, pests and timing. For a deeper look at the word, see our page on [ani meaning](/blog/ani-meaning). For the seeds behind higher yields, see [rice varieties in the Philippines](/crops/rice-varieties-philippines).

blocks.title: Where these numbers come from
blocks.text: The GDP shares come from the PSA national accounts. The 2024 and 2025 shares are our own sums of the four quarters at current prices, so they may differ a little from PSA's annual release. Job figures come from the PSA Labor Force Survey, and yields from the PSA palay and corn estimates. PSA revises its figures, so check the latest release before you quote them.

blocks.text: Questions about agriculture in the Philippine economy

items.q: What is the share of agriculture in the economy of the Philippines?
items.a: Agriculture, forestry and fishing made up about 8.6 percent of GDP in 2025 at current prices, based on PSA national accounts. In the second quarter of 2026, its share was 7.5 percent at constant prices.

items.q: How many Filipinos work in agriculture?
items.a: In July 2026, agriculture employed 19.7 percent of the 49.21 million employed persons, roughly 9.7 million people, according to the PSA Labor Force Survey.

items.q: What is the most important crop in the Philippines?
items.a: Palay. It is the country's main staple and the top contributor to farm output growth in the second quarter of 2026. Corn, coconut, banana and sugarcane follow.

items.q: What is the average palay yield per hectare?
items.a: PSA recorded 4.09 metric tons per hectare for July to September 2025. Yields vary a lot by season, variety and water supply.

items.q: Why is agriculture's share of GDP falling?
items.a: Mostly because services and industry grow faster. Farm output still grows in most quarters, but its slice of the whole economy gets smaller.
